translations.description:
Machine side lateral raises are an isolation exercise for the side (lateral) deltoids, performed on a machine for stability, targeting the outer shoulder by lifting pads or handles out to the sides to shoulder height, then lowering slowly, keeping elbows slightly bent and traps down to focus on the delts. This exercise helps build shoulder width by preventing swinging and providing constant tension, making it great for beginners or as a finisher.

How to Perform Machine Lateral Raises

Setup: Adjust the seat so your shoulders align with the machine's pivot point, your chest is against the pad (or back if facing out), and your arms are at a 90-degree angle with the pads/handles.

Starting Position: Grip the handles with a relaxed grip, elbows slightly bent, and shoulders down (depressed) away from your ears.

Lifting Phase: Exhale and lift your arms out to the sides, moving your upper arms laterally, until they are parallel to the floor.

Peak Contraction: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing the side delts, but don't shrug your shoulders up.

Lowering Phase: Inhale and slowly lower the weight back down with control, resisting the weight on the way down.
translations.name: Machine Side Lateral Raises

translations.description:
The Cable Front Raise with a small bar isolates your anterior deltoids (front shoulders) by providing constant tension, requiring you to stand facing away from a low pulley, grab the bar with an overhand grip, and lift it in front of you to shoulder height with slightly bent arms, avoiding swinging and keeping your core tight for controlled movement up and down. Use a light-to-moderate weight, focusing on slow, controlled reps to feel the muscle work, not momentum.

How to Perform the Cable Front Raise (Bar)

Setup: Attach a small straight bar to a low cable pulley. Set the weight to a light or moderate setting.

Starting Position: Stand with your back to the machine, holding the bar with an overhand grip (palms facing down) at hip level, arms extended but not locked. Feet shoulder-width apart, core braced, shoulders back and down.

The Lift: Exhale and slowly raise the bar straight up in front of you, keeping a slight bend in your elbows, until your hands reach shoulder height (or slightly below).

The Hold: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing your front delts.

The Lower: Inhale as you slowly and controllably lower the bar back to the starting position, maintaining tension.
translations.name: Cable Front Raise with a small bar

translations.description:
Technique and Execution

The Smith machine squat is a variation of the traditional barbell squat that uses a guided, fixed-path barbell. Here's a detailed breakdown of the proper technique:

Starting Position

Foot Placement: Position feet slightly forward of the bar, about shoulder-width apart

Bar Position: Rest the bar on your upper trapezius/shoulders, similar to a traditional back squat

Stance: Feet can be slightly angled outward for natural hip rotation

Squat Movement

Unrack the bar by rotating it to release from the safety hooks

Slowly lower your body by bending knees and hips

Descend until thighs are parallel to the ground (or slightly below)

Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement

Drive through your heels to return to the starting position

Benefits and Considerations

Advantages

Reduced Balance Requirements: Fixed bar path makes it easier for beginners

Controlled Movement: Less risk of improper form compared to free weight squats

Isolation: Allows focused leg muscle development
translations.name: Smith machine squat

translations.description:
Technique and Execution

Starting Position

Seated Positioning: Sit in the machine with back against the pad

Leg Placement: Inner thighs against the machine's padded resistance points

Adjust Machine: Set seat position to align your hip joint with the machine's pivot point

Movement Technique

Start with legs together or slightly pressed against the inner pads

Slowly push legs outward, spreading them apart

Move until maximum comfortable lateral range is reached

Pause briefly at the outer point of the movement

Slowly return to the starting position with controlled movement

Biomechanical Breakdown

Muscle Engagement

Primary Activation: Gluteus Medius (side hip muscle)

Stabilization: Engages core and lower back muscles

Functional Movement: Mimics lateral leg movement used in walking, sports, and daily activities

Benefits

Strength and Stability

Improves Hip Stability

Reduces Risk of Knee Injuries

Enhances Lateral Movement Capabilities

Targets Often-Neglected Muscle Groups

translations.description:
The Cable Pull Through is a lower-body exercise that targets the glutes and hamstrings using a "hip hinge" motion. To perform it, attach a rope to the lowest pulley setting, face away from the machine with the rope between your legs, and step forward to create tension. Keeping your back flat and knees slightly soft, push your hips backward as if trying to close a door behind you until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings.

To finish the rep, explosively drive your hips forward to return to a standing position, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. It is vital to remember that this is not a squat; your knees should not bend deeply, and your arms should remain straight and relaxed, acting only as hooks for the rope. This movement provides constant tension on the glutes while placing less stress on the lower back than a traditional deadlift.
translations.name: Cable pull through

translations.name: Landmine Rotation

translations.description: on a cable rack place cable high, and with a straight arm pull that cable across you from high to low. focus on tension in back shoulder.
translations.name: unilateral cross body cable pull down

translations.description:
• The barbell full squat is a compound exercise that targets multiple muscle groups in the lower body, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.
  • Proper form is crucial for maximizing results and preventing injuries during the barbell full squat. This includes maintaining a shoulder-width stance, creating whole body tension, controlling your descent, and maintaining proper depth and knee positioning.
  • Assistance moves such as the front squat, goblet squat, split squat, and Bulgarian split squat can help improve your performance in the barbell full squat by targeting specific muscle groups and improving overall technique.
  • To achieve new personal records in your back squat, gradually increase weight over time, vary rep ranges and sets to stimulate muscle growth, and prioritize rest and recovery between training sessions.
translations.name: Barbell Full Squat
notes: Start by positioning your feet shoulder-width apart, with toes slightly turned outwards.

translations.description: A combination of squat and deadlift principles with the use of a hex/trap bar, easing stress on the lower back by better centering the weight.
translations.name: Trap Bar Squat

translations.description: Move your knee forward, keeping your heel on the ground. Hold the position for a couple of seconds and return to the starting position.
translations.name: ankle dorsiflexion rocks

translations.description: Lateral raises have long been a staple for building capped delts, and lifters use everything from dumbbells and bands to machines and single-arm variations to make them grow.
translations.name: Behind the Back Cable Lateral Raise

translations.description:
1. Stand between a set of parallel bars.
  2. Place your hands, knuckles outwards, on the bars.
  3. Push down on your hands to lift yourself off the floor.
  4. Hold yourself in this position with your arms straight for the required time.
translations.name: Parallel Bar Hold
notes: Keep your body in a slightly hollow position

translations.description:
Lie face-down on a bench with your legs hanging off the edge.

  1. Bend your hips so your thighs are vertical, bending your knees at the same time so your shins stay horizontal.
  2. Straighten out your legs so they are not bent and your toes are pointing backwards horizontally.
  3. Return to the original position, and repeat.
translations.name: Reverse Hyperextension

translations.description: Lie on your stomach flat, legs extended and the backs of your feet on the ground. Bring your forearms under your shoulders, elbows directly underneath. Then press your hands into the floor to lift your chest. Draw your shoulder blades together, open your collarbones, and direct your gaze forward, while keeping the lower back relaxed.
translations.name: Sphinx

translations.description:
Basic exercise

  • Focus: enhances thoracic mobility and spinal segmentation while opening the shoulders and chest.
  • **Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Hips are square and stable, with the right knee down and the left foot forward. Lengthen your spine and align your head comfortably. Begin with your arms relaxed and open in front of your chest, palms facing each other and hands apart.
  • Inhale to initiate the movement, allowing your left arm —the one farther from the wall— to open outward and backward. Lead the twist from your thoracic spine, rotating your upper back progressively while keeping your pelvis still.
  • Exhale as you complete the rotation, guiding your left hand toward the wall as your gaze follows your hand.
  • Return by inhaling and slowly bringing your arm forward, reversing the spinal rotation segment by segment.
  • Repeat on the opposite side.

Progression

  • **Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Left knee down and right foot forward.
  • Before the basic exercise: inhale, exhalewhile moving the right arm along the wall with a circle upwards and backwards, inhalewhile bringing back the arm.
  • Basic exercise.
  • Repeat on the opposite side.
translations.name: Open Book

translations.description:
Position Side plank with the elbow and the forearm on the ground and the legs slightly bent.

Execution Lift your upper knee while keeping your feet close together, like a “shell opening,” then slowly return to the starting position. Keep your core stable and your hips aligned.
translations.name: Clamshell

translations.description:
1. Set Up: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand. Extend your arms straight up over your chest as if you were at the top of a dumbbell bench press
  2. Starting Position: Position the dumbbells so they are touching or very close together with a pronated grip (palms facing your feet and thumbs facing each other)
  3. Lowering: Without moving your upper arms or shoulders, bend your elbows and flare them outward to the sides. Lower the inner ends of the dumbbells toward the center of your chest
  4. Touch and Pause: Gently touch the dumbbells to your chest. Do not rest the weight on your body; maintain constant tension in your triceps
  5. Press: Forcefully extend your elbows to return the dumbbells to the starting position. Focus on "pushing your pinkies toward the sky" to maximize triceps engagement

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IgSjoXbpy1M&t=2
translations.name: Dumbell Tate Press
notes: Upper Arm Stability: Your upper arms should remain mostly vertical. Avoid letting your shoulders round forward or move as you bend your elbows
Keep Elbows Out: Unlike a standard press or skull crusher, the elbows must point strictly outward to the sides throughout the movement
Wrist Alignment: Keep your wrists straight and firm to prevent strain

translations.description:
"The Y"

  • Position: Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees. Lie face-down with your chest supported, keeping your head neutral or looking slightly down to avoid neck strain.
  • Grip: Hold light dumbbells with a neutral or thumbs-up grip (thumb pointing to the ceiling).
  • Movement: With straight or slightly bent elbows, raise the dumbbells up and out in a "Y" shape. Focus on moving the shoulders and shoulder blades rather than just lifting the arms.
  • Top Position: Squeeze the shoulder blades together and reach high, ensuring the arms are angled to form a "Y".
  • Control: Lower the dumbbells slowly to the starting position.
translations.name: Chest-Supported Rear Delt Raise

translations.description:
Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, chest out, and shoulders back.

Hold the resistance band with both hands, palms facing up or facing each other, depending on the band type.

Bend your elbows at a 90-degree angle and glue your upper arms to your sides.

The band should have some tension in the starting position, with your hands closer together in front of your stomach.

Rotate Outward: While keeping your elbows tucked into your sides, slowly move your hands away from each other, stretching the band.

Squeeze: Squeeze your shoulder blades together and down as you rotate your hands outward.

Range of Motion: Rotate your hands as far outward as you comfortably can without allowing your elbows to leave your sides.

Hold: Hold the end position for 1–2 seconds to maximize muscle engagement.

Return: Slowly and with control, bring your hands back to the starting position.
translations.name: Band pull-apart with external rotation
notes: Consider placing a small, rolled-up towel between your elbow and your ribs on each side to ensure your elbows stay locked at your sides.

translations.description:
Lie on your back with knees and hips bent at 90 degrees (tabletop).

Place your hands on your thighs just above your knees. Push your hands against your knees as hard as possible while using your abs to pull your knees toward your hands.

Hold for 10 seconds of maximum effort. Your abs should be shaking.
translations.name: Double-Leg Abdominal Press

translations.description: Lie on your back with knees bent. Gently pull your belly button toward your spine without moving your hips or holding your breath.
translations.name: Abdominal Draw-In

translations.description:
• Bar Position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a secure corner.

  • Stance: Stand facing the barbell with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Turn your toes out 10–35 degrees to allow for better pelvic movement and depth.

  • Grip: Cup the free end of the barbell with both hands (fingers interlaced or overlapping) and hold it at mid-chest level, just below the collarbone.

  • Descent: Brace your core and sit back into a squat, keeping your chest up and weight on your heels.

  • Depth: Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor. A good reference is when your elbows touch the tops of your thighs or just inside your knees.

  • Posture: Ensure your back remains flat and your spine neutral throughout the movement.

  • Drive: Powerfully drive through your heels to stand up. Use the momentum from your legs to "thrust" the weight upward.

  • Extension: In one fluid motion, press the bar overhead until your arms are fully extended. At the top, your biceps should be near your ears.

  • The "Lean": As you reach the top of the press, lean slightly forward into the bar to encourage proper upward rotation of the shoulder blades and avoid lower back arching.

Slowly lower the barbell back to chest height in a controlled manner before immediately beginning the next repetition.
translations.name: Landmine Squat to Press

translations.description:
1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart, holding a barbell on your upper back.
  2. Keep your back straight, chest up, and core engaged.
  3. Take a step back with one leg and lower your body by bending both knees. Ensure that your back knee nearly touches the ground.
  4. Push off your back foot to return to the starting position.
  5. Repeat the movement with the other leg.

Continue alternating between legs for the desired repetitions.
translations.name: Barbell Step Back Lunge

translations.description:
1. Sit upright in a hammerstrength decline chest press machine while squeezing your shoulder blades together and placing your heels firmly on the ground underneath your knees.
  2. The back pad should be contact with your head, shoulders, and butt at all times.
  3. Grab ahold of the handles with an overhand grip just outside shoulder-width apart just below your chest.
  4. Keeping your core braced by breathing into your stomach and flexing the abdominal muscles, push through your palms to extend your elbows while keeping them at a 45 degree angle from your torso.
  5. Once your arms are fully extended, return to the starting position.
translations.name: Hammerstrength Decline Chest Press

translations.description: Hold yourself in a support position on gymnastic rings with arms straight at sides. Focus on keeping rings turned out slightly and maintaining hollow body position. This is an isometric hold for chest, shoulders, and triceps.
translations.name: Ring Support Hold

translations.description: Lie on back with heels on floor gliders or towels. Lift hips into a bridge, then slide heels toward glutes while keeping hips elevated. Slowly return to the starting position while maintaining the hip bridge.
translations.name: Floor Glider Hamstring Curls

translations.description:
1. Hinge forwards and bend your knees slightly. Depress and retract the shoulder you will use. Rest the other hand on your knee.
  2. Raise your hand about 15 degrees overhead, maintaining the position of your shoulder.
translations.name: Trap-3 Raise

translations.description:
1. Sit with your feet pressed against each other, and one knee raised all the way out to the side of your body.
  2. Place your elbow on your raised knee, bend it at 90 degrees, and point your hand directly forward, holding your barbell/dumbbell.
  3. Keep your shoulder depressed and retracted, raise your hand until your forearm is vertical, as if you were about to wave at someone like a robot.
  4. Lower your hand to the original position and repeat.
translations.name: External Rotation Stretch
notes: Shoulders Depressed and Retracted.
If you can’t feel it, don’t up the weight because it must be ‘too easy’.

translations.description:
1. Attach a resistance band to something solid behind you. Stand away from it, holding it in your hand so it is taut.
  2. Perform the shoulder mobility and rotation drills shown in the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zdwEWchSjrI
translations.name: Banded Shoulder Drills

translations.description: See this instructive video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHwyBHS6MQs .
translations.name: Solo Hip Flexor Stretch

translations.description:
Lie on your back with one leg straight on the floor. Hold the other leg behind the knee or the back of the thigh and pull it towards your chest, keeping the knee bent, until you feel a stretch in the hamstrings.

Hold the position while breathing calmly, then switch sides.

See this instructional video from Stretch Therapy: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CrF2iMnn09w
translations.name: Bent-Leg Hamstring Stretch

translations.description:
1. Sit with your hands behind you, shoulder width apart.
  2. Lock your elbows.
  3. Scoot your feet and hips out forwards, lowering your shoulders down towards ground.
  4. Go as far as possible to obtain a good stretch.

See the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ihUAbG0e8zw
translations.name: Seated Shoulder Extension Stretch
notes: Be mindful of the elbows
Slow and controlled
Should not be painful

translations.description:
Position Side plank with the elbow and the forearm on the ground and the legs slightly bent. Stretch a doubled-up resistance band between your thighs, just above the knee.

Execution Lift your upper knee while keeping your feet close together, like a “shell opening,” then slowly return to the starting position. Keep your core stable and your hips aligned.
translations.name: Banded Clamshell

translations.description:
1. Sit in a prayer position with the soles of your feet gently pressed together.
  2. Use your hands to slowly pull your feet inwards towards your groin. Hold for as long as required.
translations.name: Butterfly Stretch
notes: Keep your back straight, don't enter a hollow position.
Push your thighs and knees downwards with your elbows if you need a better stretch.

translations.description:
1. Get on your hands and knees.
  2. Widen your knees outwards, and drop to your elbows.
  3. Without moving your elbows or knees, start to rock forwards and backwards, trying to get your bum closer to your feet.
translations.name: Frog Stretch
notes: Maintain a gentle arch in your lower back, don't let it round/hollow.
For extra challenge, hold your shins parallel and point your feet outwards at a 90 degree angle from your body,

translations.description:
1. Sit with your legs completely straight (knees locked), spread wide in a straddle position.
  2. Place your hands on the back of your neck.
  3. Hinge your torso and head towards the floor.
translations.name: Seated Pancake Good Morning
notes: Keep your back as flat as possible.
Initiate the ascent/return with your lower back, keeping your chest up.

translations.description:
1. Stand as for a squat, with your feet wide and your toes pointed slightly outwards.
  2. Gently squat into a deep, wide squat - your hips should be below your knees.
  3. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds.
  4. Come up under control, and repeat as needed.
translations.name: Horse Stance (Side Splits)
notes: Keep your back straight, as with squats.
For a better stretch, widen your stance.

translations.description:
With your legs in a sitting saddle position, push your body upwards off the ground. Your legs should be horizontal and point straight outwards. Your arms should be between your legs.

Hold isometrically as long as required.
translations.name: Straddle L-Sit
notes: Maintain a hollow body shape.
Protract and depress your shoulders, and lock your elbows.
Point your toes.

translations.description:
Sit on the ground with your legs together and your arms by your sides. Push your body off the ground using your hands, maintaining the same sitting position so that your legs are straight and your feet do not touch the floor.

Hold for as long as required.
translations.name: L-sit
notes: Keep your shoulders depressed - do not allow yourself to shrug.
Keep your arms straight.

translations.description: As with an L-sit, but allow your feet to touch the floor to support the some of the weight of your legs.
translations.name: L-Sit (Foot Supported)

translations.name: Foam Roller Anterior tibialis

translations.description:
Lie on your back with your arms stretched out to the sides and your knees bent, legs together.

Slowly lower both knees to one side while keeping your shoulders and arms on the floor. You should feel a stretch in your hips, glutes and lower back.

Hold briefly, bring your knees back to the centre and repeat on the other side.
translations.name: Hip Crossover

translations.description:
Sit on the floor and lift one foot off the ground, for example by resting that leg on the other knee.

Slowly draw circles with your foot, moving only at the ankle. Do several circles in both directions, then switch feet.
translations.name: Ankle Roll

translations.description:
Anchor a resistance band low behind you, for example at the bottom of a rack, and loop it around the front of your ankle, just above the foot.

Get into a half-kneeling position with the banded foot in front, so that the band pulls your ankle backwards.

Keeping your heel on the floor, drive your knee forward over your toes, then return under control. Repeat for several reps and switch sides.
translations.name: Banded Ankle Mobility

translations.description:
Kneel in a lunge position with one knee on the floor and the other foot in front, hands on your hips.

Keep your torso upright, squeeze the glute of the back leg and push your hips forward until you feel a stretch at the front of the hip and thigh. Hold, then switch sides.
translations.name: Hip Flexor Stretch

translations.description: View the video to undestand the exercise
translations.name: Lunge with Twist Stretch

translations.description:
Lie on your back with both knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee so that your legs form a figure four.

Reach through the gap and hold the back of the thigh of the lower leg, or its shin, and gently pull it towards your chest until you feel a stretch in the glute and outer hip of the crossed leg. Keep your head and lower back on the floor and let the crossed knee open outwards. Hold the stretch and breathe calmly, then switch sides.
translations.name: Lying Figure Four Stretch

translations.name: Banded Scapular Retraction

translations.description:
1. Set an incline bench to a 45-degree angle and sit facing the bench, chest against the pad, with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other.
  2. Position your feet firmly on the ground for stability and let your arms hang down naturally with a slight bend in your elbows.
  3. Engage your core and keep your back straight throughout the movement.
  4. Raise your arms forward and out to form a Y shape, keeping the movement controlled and your elbows slightly bent.
  5. Lift until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor and in line with your ears.
  6. Pause briefly at the top of the movement to engage your shoulder muscles fully, then slowly lower your arms back down to the starting position.
  7. Ensure the movement is slow and controlled during both the ascent and descent to maximize engagement of the deltoids and supporting muscles.
  8. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining proper form throughout.
translations.name: Incline DB Y-Raise

translations.description:
Grab two dumbbells with an overhand grip and lay your forearms across your knees.

Let your wrists flex fully, then extend your wrists.
translations.name: DB Wrist Extension

translations.description:
Stand next to a cable machine with the pulley set to waist height.

Grab the opposite-side handle with the hand farthest from the pulley, keeping your palm facing in.

Keep your core engaged, chest lifted, and shoulders relaxed. Maintain a slight bend in the elbow throughout the lift.

Lift your arm out to the side until your elbow reaches shoulder height, keeping your wrist aligned with your elbow.

Briefly pause at the top, then slowly lower the handle back to your side with control. Repeat for the desired reps.
translations.name: High-Cable Lateral Raise

translations.description:
• Starting Position: Sit on the floor with both hips and knees bent at 90-degree angles.
  • Leg Placement: Place one leg in front of you (external rotation) and the other leg out to the side/behind you (internal rotation). The shins and knees should remain flat on the ground.
  • The Movement: Keeping your hips square, hinge your torso forward or tilt it laterally (side-to-side) toward the front leg to deepen the stretch.
  • Target Areas: Stretches the glutes and piriformis (front leg) and the hip flexors and quads (back leg). Engages the core and obliques during lateral flexion.
  • Goal: Improves hip mobility, specifically internal and external rotation, and relieves lower back tension.
translations.name: Shinbox IR Stretch

translations.description:
• Purpose: Improves shoulder stability, posture, and scapular (shoulder blade) control. Often used in physical therapy and warm-ups.
  • Starting Position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips (like a deadlift) keeping your back flat, or lie face down on an incline bench. Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout.
  • Y (Arms up): Extend both arms straight forward and upward at a 135-degree angle from your body, forming a "Y". Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
  • T (Arms out): Open your arms straight out to the sides, perpendicular to your body, forming a "T". Focus on pinching your shoulder blades.
  • W (Arms bent): Pull your elbows back, bending them to 90 degrees, and squeeze your shoulder blades to form a "W". Keep your wrists firm.
  • L (Arms rotated): Start with elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your body. Rotate your forearms outward (external rotation) like a goalpost, forming an "L" or a gate.
  • Key Focus: Movements should be slow and controlled. Always lead with the thumbs and think about moving the shoulder blades, not just the arms.
translations.name: YTWL Exercise

translations.description:
• Starting Position: Lie on your back (supine) on a mat, with your legs extended and relaxed. Arms can be placed alongside your body or out to the sides for stability.
  • The Movement: Slightly lift one leg off the floor (keeping it straight or with a slight bend). Move it laterally outward, away from the other leg, as if stepping over a small obstacle.
  • Range of Motion: Move the leg as far as comfortable without lifting your pelvis or rotating your torso, feeling a stretch in the inner thigh and hip.
  • Return: Slowly bring the leg back to the starting position with controlled movement.
  • Goal: Improves lateral hip mobility (abduction) and strengthens the pelvic stabilizer muscles.
translations.name: Supine Hip Abduction

translations.description:
• Setup: Lie on a decline bench with your head at the top and grip the handles.
  • The Start: Extend legs fully, keeping them slightly elevated to engage your core.
  • The Lift: Raise your legs toward the ceiling using your abs, not momentum.
  • The Squeeze: Pause and contract your lower abdominals at the top.
  • The Return: Lower your legs slowly to the starting position with control.
translations.name: Decline Bench Leg Raise

translations.description:
• Setup: Stand with feet together and grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders.
  • Position: Rest the bar on your upper chest.
  • Press: Brace your core and push the bar straight up until your arms lock out.
  • Finish: Control the bar back down to your chest.
  • https://youtu.be/ZXpdJOLNoWw?si=u27cGyODoblXHBu1
translations.name: Overhead Barbell Press

translations.description:
• Setup: Stand facing the cable, feet shoulder-width apart, with a slight forward lean.
  • Grip: Hold the rope with palms facing each other and elbows tucked tight to your ribs.
  • Execution: Push the rope down until arms are fully straight, pulling the ends apart at the bottom.
  • Control: Keep upper arms still and return to the start with a slow, controlled motion.
translations.name: Tricep Rope Pushdowns

translations.description:
• The First Pull: Lift the bar from the floor to knee-height by driving with the legs, keeping the angle of your back constant.
  • The "Power" Position: As the bar reaches mid-thigh, explosively shrug and extend your hips to create vertical momentum.
  • The Quick Elbow Turnover: In the catch phase, rotate your elbows rapidly under the bar to create a "shelf" on your front deltoids.
  • The Vertical Press: Press the bar in a straight line; your head should shift slightly forward once the bar clears your forehead to reach full lockout.
translations.name: Clean and Press

translations.description:
• Setup: Begin in a standard plank position with a weight plate balanced securely on your upper back.
  • Alignment: Maintain a straight line from your head to your heels, engaging your core to prevent your back from sagging.
  • Execution: Lower your body until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your elbows at a forty-five degrees.
  • Ascent: Press through your palms to return to the starting position, fully extending your arms.
translations.name: Weighted push-ups

translations.description: Pectoral issolation exercise - full range of motion is best with full contraction and slow negative
translations.name: Pec Deck

translations.description: Set weight and grip for the cables in the cage. Take a few steps away, bend over, pull and extend the back at the same time.
translations.name: Pullback

translations.description:
Get into bridge position, balance yourself on heels and start extending legs unilaterally.

Keep hip extended as much as possible.
translations.name: Hip Bridge

translations.description: No stops during movement, hands on the hips.
translations.name: Unilateral Lunges

translations.description: Lie on stomach, intertwine fingers behind the head and start raising your head and raise elbows as far as they go.
translations.name: Butterfly Superman

translations.description:
Lay on the back and lift legs in perpendicular fashion, keeping the knees together.

Start making small circles in one direction with both of your knees with very small range of motion, focusing on abs and keeping your back in contact with the floor.
translations.name: Leg Wheel

translations.description:
• Push one foot back until leg fully extended, concentrating on the having the foot high and pushed back as if pulled.

  • Extend arm forward with focus having the shoulder high up.

Unilateral and static hold.
translations.name: Kneeling Superman

translations.description: On your fours and raise the knees of the floor ever so slightly.  Curl your back out and push back from your shoulders as to resemble a cat making itself look large.
translations.name: Cat Plank

translations.description: Sit back, raise feet above the ground with knees bent and start rotating left and right with hands touching the ground every move.
translations.name: Core Rotation

translations.description: Extend one leg while laying down and start raising your body with one leg touching the ground through the heel.
translations.name: Unilateral Hip Thrust

translations.description: The parallel bars isometric hold is a static upper-body exercise performed on dip bars (parallel bars). Instead of moving up and down like in a traditional dip, you hold a fixed position under tension.
translations.name: Isometria alle parallele

translations.description:
Distribute your body weight evenly on all knees and arms. Keep the torso stable, with the abdomen engaged and the lumbar spine straight without twisting the back (imagine: a glass on your lower back won't fall off). Raise one leg outwards without twisting it.

Pay attention to the right angle at the hips and knees. Always train both sides of the body.

To increase resistance, a resistance band can be used.
translations.name: Quadruped Hip Abduction

translations.description: Basic calisthenics progression for the full planche
translations.name: Tuck planche

translations.description: Plate-loaded chest press machine from Legend Fitness LeverEdge line.
translations.name: Legend Chest Press

translations.description: Deep loaded stretch for pectorals, typically performed at end of chest work.
translations.name: Extreme Pec Stretch

translations.description: Deep loaded stretch for deltoids, performed after pressing movements.
translations.name: Extreme Shoulder Stretch

translations.description: Deep loaded stretch for latissimus dorsi, performed after pulling movements.
translations.name: Extreme Lat Stretch

translations.description:
1. Place a bench between two cable pulleys and adjust the pulleys so they are at chest/shoulder height when you are seated.
  2. Grab the handles with a neutral grip and lean against the upright backrest.
  3. Bring your arms together in front of your chest in a controlled motion, focusing on squeezing your chest muscles. Keep your elbows slightly bent throughout the movement.
  4. Pause briefly at the top position.
  5. Slowly lower your arms back to the starting position while maintaining control of the movement.
  6. Repeat for reps.
translations.name: Seated Cable chest fly

translations.description:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder width apart holding the barbell with both hands in front just past shoulder width.
  2. Bend forward at the hips with a slight bend in your knees, keeping your back straight.
  3. Engage your shoulder blades, as if you are trying to touch them together.
  4. Release the shrug. Description taken from MuscleWiki
translations.name: Barbell Silverback Shrug

translations.description: The Inverted Lat Pull Down (most commonly known as the Reverse Grip Lat Pull Down) is a variation of the standard exercise that uses an underhand (supinated) grip with hands at shoulder-width. This position shifts more emphasis to the lower lats and increases biceps involvement, often allowing for a greater range of motion and a deeper squeeze at the bottom of the movement.
translations.name: Inverted Lat Pull Down

translations.description: The Seated V-Grip Row is a compound pulling exercise performed on a cable machine using a close-grip "V" handle. While seated with your feet braced, you pull the handle toward your midsection, focusing on back thickness and mid-back development.
translations.name: Seated V-Grip Row

translations.description: The Assisted Pull-Up is a compound vertical pulling exercise performed on a machine with a counterweight platform or by using resistance bands. It mimics the mechanics of a standard pull-up but reduces the total weight you have to lift, making it an excellent tool for building functional strength and perfecting your technique.
translations.name: Assisted Pull-Up

translations.description: The Dumbbell Curl is a classic isolation exercise for the arms. Unlike the Hammer Curl, it involves rotating your wrists (supination) as you lift the weights, which allows for a full contraction of the biceps.
translations.name: Dumbbell Curl

translations.description: The Abdominal Crunch is a classic core isolation exercise performed on the floor or a mat. Unlike a full sit-up, it involves a smaller range of motion where you only lift your shoulders and upper back off the ground, keeping your lower back pressed firmly against the floor.
translations.name: Abdominal Crunch

translations.description: Belt Squat: a squat variation done with a belt attached to a loading machine or platform so the weight is supported at the hips instead of on the spine. It mainly trains the quads and glutes, with much less lower-back fatigue than a barbell squat. Use a full range of motion, keep the torso upright, and drive through the mid-foot.
translations.name: Belt Squat

translations.description: Cable rear delt fly (single arm): Stand sideways to a cable machine with the handle set around shoulder height. With a slight bend in the elbow, pull the handle out and back in a wide arc so the upper arm moves away from the body. Keep your torso still and focus on the rear delt doing the work. Use light to moderate weight and controlled reps.
translations.name: Cable Rear-Delt Fly (single arm)

translations.description: On all fours. Arch spine up (cat) then drop it down (cow). Breathe with movement.
translations.name: Cat-Cow

translations.description: Controlled Articular Rotations. Slow full circles 3 each way. Cervical mobility.
translations.name: Neck CARs

translations.description: Belly breathing. Hand on chest stays still, hand on belly rises. 8-10 slow breaths.
translations.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing

translations.description:
Key Steps to Execute Correctly:

Setup: Place the dumbbell between your feet, with your shoulders above your hips, chest up, and back flat.

The Pull: Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles (triple extension) to drive the dumbbell upward, keeping your elbow high and the dumbbell close to your body.

The Catch: Quickly flex your hips and knees to drop under the dumbbell and receive it overhead with your arm locked in position, landing in a half-squat stance.

Common Mistakes: Using your arms too much to lift the weight instead of your legs, having a low elbow during the pull phase, and misaligning your shoulder, elbow, and wrist in the final position. For beginners, it’s recommended to start with light loads, focus on technique, and perform 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps per arm.
translations.name: dumbbell snatch

translations.description: This exercise requires a sturdy box or a chair. Simple stand ~6 inches in front of it and balance yourself on one leg. From here, begin squatting down in a smooth controlled motion while keeping your other leg straight out in front of you for balance. Slowly sit down on the box, pause for a 1 count and push back up with the working leg, while never letting your other leg touch the ground.
translations.name: 1 Leg Box Squat

translations.description:
The Step Jack is a low-impact plyometric-style move that provides cardiovascular benefits without the joint stress of jumping. It works the entire body, specifically targeting the legs, core, and shoulders. This move is ideal for beginners, individuals with joint sensitivities, or as a dynamic warm-up to gradually elevate the heart rate. Notes (Instructions):

  1. ​Stand upright with your feet together and arms at your sides.
  2. ​Step your right foot out to the side while simultaneously swinging both arms up above your head.
  3. Bring your right foot back to the center and lower your arms.
  4. ​Immediately repeat the movement, stepping out with your left foot.
  5. ​Continue alternating sides at a steady, rhythmic pace.
translations.name: Step Jack

translations.description:
​A tempo-based squat that uses controlled movement to increase muscle tension and improve lower-body stability.

  1. ​Lower: Descend slowly for 3 seconds.
  2. ​Pause: Hold at the bottom for 1 second.
  3. ​Stand: Return to the starting position at a normal pace.
  4. Form: Keep your chest up and weight in your heels.
translations.name: Slow Squat

translations.description:
​A push-up variation with a wider hand placement to increase the emphasis on the outer chest muscles and shoulders.

  1. ​Setup: Place hands wider than shoulder-width apart on the floor.
  2. Lower: Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your core tight.
  3. ​Push: Drive through your palms to return to the start position.
  4. ​Form: Don't let your lower back sag; keep a straight line from head to heels.
translations.name: Wide Push-Up

translations.description:
A low-impact cardio and mobility exercise that strengthens the hip flexors and improves balance.

  1. ​Movement: Stand tall and lift one knee toward your chest as high as comfortable.
  2. ​Arms: Swing the opposite arm forward as you lift your knee, similar to a walking motion.
  3. ​Core: Keep your abs engaged to maintain an upright posture.
  4. ​Pace: Perform the movement with control, alternating legs rhythmically.
translations.name: Marching High Knees

translations.description:
• Begin in a half kneeling position with the leg away from the wall stabilized against the wall with a ball.
  • With both hands directly in front of you, rotate one arm open attempting to reach the wall behind you.
  • Exhale as you rotate, inhale as you return to neutral and repeat.
translations.name: 1/2 Kneeling Thoracic Rotation
notes: You will feel the mid-back and shoulder open with this exercise.
Avoid rotating from your lower back. The motion should primarily be occurring in your mid-back

translations.description: slow controlled seated forward exercise with dumbbells
translations.name: lento avanti seduto

translations.description: Press the dumbbell vertically overhead in a controlled motion until your arm is fully extended, without locking the elbow. Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position at shoulder height.
translations.name: Single-arm dumbbell shoulder press
notes: Keep your core tight throughout the movement to avoid lateral trunk lean
Do not arch your lower back as you press
Keep your wrist neutral and aligned with your forearm
Control the descent — do not drop the weight

translations.description: Single-arm cable pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise that targets the triceps brachii. By working one arm at a time, it helps correct strength imbalances between sides while also engaging the core for stability. Starting position: Stand facing the cable machine with your feet shoulder-width apart. Attach a single handle to the high pulley. Grab the handle with one hand using an overhand grip (pronated), with your elbow bent at approximately 90° and tucked close to your body. Keep your core braced and your back straight. Execution: Push the handle downward in a controlled motion by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended. Hold the contraction for 1 second at the bottom, then slowly return to the starting position.
translations.name: Single-arm cable pushdown
notes: Keep your elbow fixed and close to your body throughout the movement
Do not swing your torso or use momentum
Control the return — do not let the weight pull your arm up
Keep your wrist neutral and firm

translations.description:
A compound exercise combining elements of a sumo deadlift and a high pull. It targets the posterior chain, particularly the glutes, hamstrings, and upper back. The sumo stance increases hip engagement, while the high pull adds an explosive element, promoting power development.

  • Stand upright overtop of a kettlebell with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart angled out slightly.
  • Maintain a braced core and neutral spine throughout the exercise.
  • Hinge your hips backward and extend your arms to grab ahold the kettlebell with a double overhand grip.
  • With you lower legs nearly vertical to the ground, extend your hips to raise the kettlebell with your elbows high keeping it close to your body.
  • Once the kettlebell has reached shoulder height, lower back to the starting position.
translations.name: Kettlebell sumo high pull

translations.description: Close grip front facing Pull down, while focusing on Biceps, Increases activation of biceps over the whole range, Avoid activating Lats.
translations.name: Mentzer Pulldown

translations.description: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grab the single handle with a neutral grip. Keep your torso stable, your chest lifted, and your shoulder blades slightly retracted. Start with your arm fully extended overhead, then pull the handle down toward your upper chest following a controlled, slightly diagonal path. Focus on engaging the latissimus dorsi while keeping the shoulder depressed and avoiding any torso rotation. Slowly return to the starting position, maintaining full control throughout the movement.
translations.name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
notes: Keep the shoulder down and away from the ear during the entire movement.
Avoid leaning or twisting your torso to assist the pull.
Control the eccentric phase and avoid letting the weight pull you upward.
Focus on pulling with the back muscles, not with the biceps.
Keep the elbow close to the body in the final part of the pull.

translations.description:
Stand on one leg and lean your upper body slightly forward while keeping your back straight. Extend the free leg behind you so that your torso and leg form roughly one line. Slowly open your hip to the side by rotating your pelvis and upper body in a controlled way. Then close the hip again and return to the starting position.

The movement should mainly come from the hip. Keep your standing foot stable and avoid letting your knee collapse inward.
translations.name: Hip Airplane

translations.description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your knees stacked on top of each other. Keep your feet together at first, then keep your knees touching while lifting your top foot upward. Slowly lower the foot back down with control.

Move only through the hip and avoid rolling your pelvis backward. The movement should be small, controlled, and focused on hip rotation.
translations.name: Reverse Clamshell

translations.description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your legs stacked. Lift your top knee into a clamshell position and keep the leg elevated throughout the movement. From there, alternate between opening the knee upward and lifting the foot upward, moving through hip external and internal rotation.

Keep the movement slow and controlled. Do not let the top leg rest on the bottom leg between repetitions.
translations.name: Clamshell to Reverse Clamshell

translations.description:
This is a variation of the flat bench press designed to emphasize the clavicular head of the pectoralis major (the upper portion). By tilting the torso, the angle of the push changes, shifting more tension to the upper chest and shoulders, which helps achieve a more aesthetic, balanced, and three-dimensional development of the torso.

  1. Starting Position: Grip a bar with an overhand grip (palms facing up) at a width similar to your shoulders.

  2. Position on the Bench: Kneel in front of a flat bench and rest the backs of your forearms on it. Your wrists and hands should extend slightly beyond the edge of the bench to allow for a full range of motion.

  3. Eccentric Phase (Lowering): Lower the bar in a controlled manner by extending your wrists toward the floor. At the bottom of the movement, slightly spread your fingers to let the bar roll down a bit, maximizing the stretch.

  4. Concentric Phase (Lift): First, close your fingers to secure the bar, then flex your wrists upward explosively but in a controlled manner, bringing the bar as high as possible. Strongly contract your forearms at the top position for one second.

  5. Form: Keep your forearms firmly pressed against the bench throughout the exercise; only your wrists and fingers should move.
translations.name: Curl De Muñeca Con Barra

translations.description: The YTW exercise for scapular retraction is designed to strengthen the inter-scapular muscles between your shoulder blades, to help retract or pull your shoulders back, helping to maintain proper upright posture.
translations.name: YTW Raises
notes: Start in neutral standing posture.
Bring your arms up to roughly 135 degrees for the Y position, slightly in front of you, then bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Concentrate on squeezing the shoulder blade or scapula contraction at the end range of motion, holding this position for 3-5 seconds. Then release.
Bring your arms down to roughly 90 degrees, rotate your thumbs outwards, and bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades again with scapular retraction.
For the W component, keep your arms around 90 degrees, but bring them backwards in a slight W position
squeezing at the end range-focusing on the middle and lower inter-scapular fibers.

translations.description: Kneel on a glute-ham developer or have a partner hold your ankles. Keeping hips straight, lower your torso toward the floor under control, then curl back up by contracting the hamstrings and glutes.
translations.name: Glute-Ham Raise

translations.description: Swim freestyle at a relaxed, steady pace without stopping — think conversation pace, not racing. Focus on smooth, even strokes rather than speed or breathing technique; this is just to get your body moving and your heart rate up.
translations.name: Easy Continuous Swim (Freestyle)

translations.description: Hold a kickboard with both hands, arms extended in front of you, face in the water (lift head forward to breathe when needed). Kick from your hips, not your knees, keeping your legs mostly straight with a slight bend and a steady, compact flutter kick. This builds leg endurance and keeps your body horizontal without needing to worry about your arms.
translations.name: Kick with Board

translations.description: Stand in chest-deep water. Take a breath, submerge your face fully, and exhale slowly and completely through your nose and/or mouth the whole time you're underwater — a gentle humming sound can help keep the exhale steady and controlled. Once you're empty of air, lift your head, take a fresh breath, and go back under. Repeat continuously. The goal is training your body that all your exhaling happens underwater, so all you need to do at the surface is inhale.
translations.name: Bobbing Exhale Drill

translations.description: Hold the pool wall or edge with one hand, body horizontal at the surface, legs kicking gently behind you. Keep your face in the water, exhaling continuously, then rotate your head to the side — not lifting it up — so one goggle stays in the water while the other clears the surface. Take a quick breath, then rotate your face back down to neutral. This isolates the head-rotation motion without any arm strokes to think about.
translations.name: Wall-Hold Rotation

translations.description: Push off the wall on your side (not flat on your stomach), one arm extended forward holding the board or just extended, kicking continuously. Keep your head in a neutral position looking at the bottom of the pool, and when you need air, rotate your head sideways (one ear stays in the water, other faces up) to breathe, then rotate back to neutral. Swim a length like this, then repeat on the other side. This teaches the exact head position and rotation you'll use once full stroke breathing comes in.
translations.name: Side-Kick Breathing (Kickboard)

translations.description: Push off, swim a few strokes, and every breath roll fully onto your back for 2-3 breaths, then roll back into freestyle. This teaches you to rotate your body as a unit rather than just turning your head, and helps remove the fear of not having your face in the water.
translations.name: Stroke-and-Roll Drill

translations.description: Same motion as the Bobbing Exhale Drill, but done in slightly deeper water (so you're not touching the bottom) and at a slower, more relaxed pace — think of it as a recovery/reset exercise rather than a hard drill. Use it between harder drills to reset your breathing rhythm and calm down if you're feeling rushed or out of sync.
translations.name: Recovery Bobbing

translations.description: Swim at an easy, unhurried pace — freestyle, backstroke, or just floating/gliding — with zero focus on technique or drills. The only goal here is to let your heart rate come down gradually and your muscles relax before you get out of the pool.
translations.name: Cool-Down Swim

aliases: Pelvic Tilt Drill / Supine Pelvic Tilt
translations.description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Flatten your lower back against the floor by tilting your pelvis posteriorly, engaging your abs and glutes. Hold 5 seconds, release. This retrains pelvic positioning to counter anterior pelvic tilt.
translations.name: Posterior Pelvic Tilt

translations.description: This is an end range strengthening exercise for the knee extensors. Start by looping a band around the back of one knee and anchoring the other end to a stable surface in front of you. Stand in a split stance with the banded knee bent and placed as the front leg. Straighten the knee to pull against the bands resistance and maintain a contraction in your quadriceps for up to 5 seconds before releasing.
translations.name: Band Terminal Knee extension

translations.description:
1. Stand facing a wall. Place your forearms vertically against the wall so your elbows and wrists are both touching it.
  2. Point your arms slightly outwards from "straight up".
  3. Protract your shoulders hard, then slide your forearms up the wall until your elbows are about level with your chin.
  4. Slide your forearms back down the wall. Repeat as necessary.
translations.name: Serratus Wall Slide Stretch
notes: Keep a hollow body position; don't allow your back to arch.
Keep your shoulders protracted through the movement.

translations.description:
1. Stand facing away from a bench, couch or similar-height object.
  2. Extend one leg backwards, resting your foot "laces-down" on the edge of the bench.
  3. Lower yourself until your rear knee is on the floor and you are in a lunge position, with your torso hanging forwards slightly.
  4. Brace your core, tense your rear glute, and straighten up your torso to vertical, under control. Relax and repeat.

Repeat for the other leg, too.
translations.name: Couch Stretch

translations.description:
1. Hold the resistance band (or any other rope-like object, the elasticity is not necessary) above your head, between your hands, with your arms straight. Pull it taught to engage your lats.
  2. Step forwards into a lunge, dropping until your knee is almost touching the floor.
  3. Slowly and controlledly pulse your body up and down by about an inch. Repeat for required reps.
  4. Repeat for other leg.
translations.name: Long Lunge Pulse Stretch

translations.description:
1. Start kneeling.
  2. Extend one leg out forwards, fully straightened. Follow with your hips so your back leg begins to unfold.
  3. Carefully lower yourself into the stretch. Do not go beyond your limit.
  4. Hold for the required time.
translations.name: Front Split Stretch
notes: Keep your body upright and straight throughout.
Keep your hips square throughout.

translations.description:
1. Drop into a squat.
  2. Hold one ankle with the opposite hand.
  3. Fold your other arm to your chest.
  4. Staying in the squat and keeping hold of your ankle, twist to turn your chest-hand back/outwards until your elbow is pointing at the sky.
  5. Return to the neutral squatting position with your hand on your chest. Repeat movement as required.

Repeat on both sides.
translations.name: Squat Sky Reach Stretch
notes: If you can, at the top of the stretch uncoil your arm and reach your hand for the sky, returning your hand to your chest on the way down.

translations.description:
Explosive Push-Ups

Start in a standard push-up position, lower your chest, then explosively push off the ground so your hands leave the floor. Land softly and immediately repeat.
translations.name: Explosive Push-Ups

translations.description:
Russian Push-Ups

Start in a standard push-up position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Lower your chest toward the floor, then shift your body forward while keeping your chest close to the ground. Extend your arms to return to the starting position, then reverse the movement smoothly. Keep your core tight and maintain controlled movement throughout the exercise.
translations.name: Russian Push Ups

translations.description: ​A calisthenics static balance skill where the entire body is held straight and parallel to the ground, supported by tucking the elbows firmly into the abdomen or pelvic bones.
translations.name: elbow lever

translations.description: A straight-arm calisthenics static hold where you assume a plank position and lean the shoulders as far forward as possible past the wrists with protracted scapulae and a hollow body.
translations.name: Planche Lean Hold

translations.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C995b3KLXS4&t=7s

  • Elbows should stay straight
  • Hold it for time/reps
  • Start at an active hang: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HoE-C85ZlCE
  • Progress towards a 90 degree in your shoulder
translations.name: Arch Hang

translations.description: An isometric leg extension is a strengthening exercise where you contract your quadriceps muscles against an immovable resistance without changing the length of the muscle or moving your knee joint.
translations.name: Leg Extension Isometric

translations.description: A bench press isometric hold is a static strength exercise where you pause and hold a barbell or dumbbells either at your chest, mid-press, or at lockout without moving for a set time
translations.name: Bench Press Isometric

translations.description: An isometric overhead press involves holding a weight statically overhead or pushing against an immovable object at a specific point in the press without moving the joint.
translations.name: Overhead Press Isometric

translations.description: An isometric lateral raise is a shoulder exercise where you hold your arms out to the sides at waist height for a set amount of time instead of moving up and down
translations.name: Lateral Raise Isometric

translations.description: An isometric preacher curl is a static strength exercise where you hold a fixed position on a preacher pad or and inclined bench under tension without moving the joint.
translations.name: Preacher Curl Isometric

translations.description: An isometric Lat pulldown is a strength-building exercise where you pull the bar down to your chest and hold the contracted position at the bottom without moving your limbs for a set number of seconds
translations.name: Lat Pulldown Isometric

translations.description: A single-arm isometric or isolated triceps pushdown is an isolation cable exercise where you pin your upper arm against your torso, hinge at the hips, and extend the elbow to achieve a peak contraction in the triceps muscle.
translations.name: Triceps Pushdown Isometric

translations.description: Bag workout for boxing skill development and cardio improvement
translations.name: Boxing

translations.description: Wrist circles is warm-up exercise, where you rotate your wrists in a circular motion. They improve mobility and are recommended before exercises such as pull ups, hand stands and other exercises that put pressure on your wrists.
translations.name: Wrist circles
notes: Rotate one time in both directions per rep

translations.description: Controlled treadmill walking performed backward, at a slow and steady speed. A slight incline of about 2 to 3 percent can be added if tolerated.
translations.name: Retro Treadmill Walking

translations.description:
Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit upright in a chair. Locate the pelvic floor muscles: they are the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or to hold back gas. Keep your abdomen, glutes and thighs relaxed and breathe normally throughout.

Tighten the pelvic floor muscles and lift them gently upwards and inwards. Hold the contraction for a few seconds, then release completely and rest for at least as long as you held. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

The exercise can be varied by holding longer with a light contraction (endurance) or by performing quick, short contractions with a full relaxation in between.
translations.name: Kegel Exercise

translations.description:
Stand in a split stance with one foot about a stride in front of the other, and hold on to a stable support such as a rack, a wall or the back of a chair.

Lower your hips straight down by bending both knees until the back knee almost touches the floor. Keep your upper body upright and the front heel on the floor, then push through the front foot back up. Use the support only for balance, not to pull yourself up. Complete all repetitions, then switch sides.
translations.name: Supported Split Squat

translations.description: Controlled breathing drill performed in a 90/90 position to encourage rib, abdominal, and pelvic coordination.
translations.name: 90/90 Breathing

translations.description:
Sit on the floor with one leg bent at 90 degrees in front of you and the other leg bent at 90 degrees out to the side, so that the rear shin is parallel to the front shin. Keep your torso upright and, if possible, your hands off the floor.

Rotate both knees over to the other side so that the legs swap positions and you arrive in the same 90/90 position facing the opposite way. Move slowly and under control, keeping the feet in contact with the floor, and alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions.

Mobility drill for internal and external rotation of the hips.
translations.name: 90/90 Hip Switches

translations.description:
Start on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips. Extend one leg straight out to the side with the foot flat on the floor and the toes pointing forward.

Keep your back flat and slowly push your hips back towards the heel of the kneeling leg until you feel a stretch along the inside of the extended leg. Pause briefly, then return to the starting position. Complete all repetitions on one side before switching legs.

Mobility exercise for the adductors and the hips.
translations.name: Adductor Rock Backs

translations.description:
Stand facing a bar, box or bench at roughly hip height and place the heel of one leg on it. Keep that leg straight with the toes pointing up, and keep the standing leg straight with both hips square to the support.

Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in the back of the elevated thigh. Hold the position while breathing calmly, then switch legs.

Stretch for the hamstrings. The height of the support controls the intensity: the higher the leg, the stronger the stretch.
translations.name: Elevated Hamstring Stretch

translations.description:
Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.

Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
  • Improves Balance: Standing on one leg challenges your stability.
  • Enhances Coordination: Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.
  • Strengthens Core: The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.
How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
  1. Positioning: Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.
  2. Balance: Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.
  3. Duration: Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.
Progression Tips
  • Add Movement: Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.
  • Close Your Eyes: This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.
  • Use a Ball: Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.

This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.
translations.name: Single-leg BOSU balance

translations.description:
What Are Quad Sets?

Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.

How to Perform Quad Sets Steps to Execute Quad Sets
  1. Positioning: Sit or lie down with your legs straight.
  2. Tightening: Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.
  3. Holding: Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.
  4. Releasing: Relax the muscle after the hold.
  5. Repetitions: Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.
Tips for Effective Quad Sets
  • Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.
  • Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.
  • It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.
Benefits of Quad Sets
  • Restores Muscle Function: Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.
  • Improves Stability: Enhances stability in the knee joint.
  • Increases Range of Motion: Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.

Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.
translations.name: Quad Sets

translations.description:
Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.

Exercise Descriptions Hip-Out Steps
  • Movement: Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.
  • Target Muscles: Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.
  • Benefits: Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.
Hip-In Steps
  • Movement: Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.
  • Target Muscles: Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.
  • Benefits: Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.
Key Benefits of Lateral Steps

| Benefit | Description | |---|---| | Strengthening Hip Abductors | Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. | | Enhancing Stability | Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. | | Improving Coordination | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |

Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.
translations.name: Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

translations.description:
Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.

Overview

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.

Benefits
  • Improves balance: Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.
  • Enhances proprioception: Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.
  • Supports rehabilitation: Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.
How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds Steps
  1. Preparation: Stand on a stable surface or a box.
  2. Takeoff: Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.
  3. Landing: Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.
  4. Hold position: Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.
  5. Reset: Return to the starting position and repeat.
Key Points to Remember
  • Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.
  • Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.
  • Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.
Conclusion

Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.
translations.name: Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

translations.description:
Step into the V-squat machine facing the pad, the opposite way from the regular V-squat, so that your chest rests against the pad and your shoulders sit under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform about shoulder width apart and release the safety.

Brace your core and lower yourself by bending your knees and pushing the hips back until your thighs are roughly parallel to the platform. Drive back up through the heels without locking out the knees.

Compared to the regular V-squat, the reversed position shifts the emphasis towards the glutes and hamstrings.
translations.name: Reverse V-Squat

translations.description: Pike push-up with legs on an elevated surface. Progression to handstand push-up.
translations.name: Box Handstand Push-up

translations.description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet about hip-width apart, holding one end in each hand in front of your thighs. Keeping your arms straight with a slight bend in the elbows, raise your hands forward to shoulder height, then lower slowly under control. Can be done with both arms together or alternating. Use a heavier band or shorten the band to increase resistance.
translations.name: Banded Front Raise
notes: Stand on more of the band to increase resistance.
Lower under control instead of letting the band snap back.
Keep a slight, fixed bend in the elbows throughout.
Stop at shoulder height; going higher shifts the work to the traps.

translations.description: Sit at a plate-loaded (lever) lat pulldown machine with your thighs secured under the pads. Grip the handles overhead with arms fully extended. Pull the handles down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, squeezing your lats at the bottom. Return slowly to full extension. Resistance comes from weight plates loaded on the machine's lever arms rather than a cable stack.
translations.name: Plate-Loaded Lat Pulldown
notes: Keep the torso near vertical; leaning back turns it into a row.
Let the arms extend fully at the top of each rep.
Set the seat so the handles start above your head with arms fully extended.
Drive the elbows down and back rather than pulling with the hands.

translations.description: Set a cable pulley at the lowest position and attach a single handle. Stand side-on to the machine, hold the frame with your near hand and lean your body away so you hang at an angle. With the far hand, grasp the handle in front of your hips and raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower slowly. The lean increases tension on the side delts at the bottom of the movement. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
translations.name: Lean-Away Cable Lateral Raise
notes: Raise to shoulder height, no higher.
The lean is what keeps tension on the side delt at the bottom.
Hold the frame firmly and let your body hang away at a steady angle.
Lead with the elbow, keeping a slight bend in it.

translations.description:
Adjust the seat so that your armpits rest on the top edge of the pad and your upper arms lie flat on it. Grip the handles with your palms facing up.

Curl the handles up by bending your elbows, without lifting your upper arms off the pad or leaning back. Squeeze the biceps briefly at the top, then lower the handles slowly until your arms are almost straight.
translations.name: Preacher Curl Machine

translations.description: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.
translations.name: Seated Band Row
notes: Keep the torso still; don't rock backward to finish the rep.
Shorten your grip on the band for more resistance.
Sit tall: hips stacked under the shoulders, chest up.
Pull to the lower ribs, not the chest.

translations.description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.
translations.name: FlexBar Wrist Extension
notes: Use a lighter bar if you feel it in the elbow joint rather than the forearm muscles.
Rest the forearm on your thigh so only the wrist moves.
Lower over about three seconds; the slow part matters most.

translations.description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing up and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist extend back, then curl the wrist up to raise the bar while the forearm stays still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. Works the wrist flexors, and is the companion movement to FlexBar wrist extension for balanced forearm strengthening.
translations.name: FlexBar Wrist Flexion
notes: Palm faces up; the forearm stays flat on the thigh.
Curl the wrist, don't lift the arm.
Pair with wrist extension so both sides of the forearm get worked.

translations.description: An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.
translations.name: FlexBar Tyler Twist
notes: The working wrist does the slow unwinding; the other hand just holds position.
Take about four seconds to let the bar untwist.
Mild discomfort in the forearm is expected; sharp joint pain is not.
Reverse the twist direction to target the flexors for golfer's elbow.
